title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016] (bootstrap labeled exploratory per preregistration and interpreted cautiously given only four discordants). Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative validator traces, and give explicit artifact pointers and hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Operator intent→device configuration translation aims to reduce manual NetOps effort but risks outages when generated CLI sequences or transient change orders violate workflow, availability, or dependency constraints. Large language models (LLMs) can produce device configurations from high‑level intent but are prone to hallucinations and erroneous sequences that are operationally unsafe. A pragmatic mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration using an LLM, deterministically verify the candidate against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, issue a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We contribute: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) a precise, artifact‑grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and an explicitly labeled exploratory paired bootstrap CI with a small‑discordant caveat; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a discussion of verifier blind spots and operational limits.
sections.related_work: Three literatures motivate this study. Surveys and system papers document LLM‑assisted NetOps (intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps, multi‑agent orchestration) while highlighting hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers [Nguyen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Long et al., 2025]. Methodological work on tool‑augmented LLMs and generate–validate–repair stresses standardized evaluation for RAG-style pipelines and quantification of verifier coverage and operational costs [Simon et al., 2024; Confucius framework, 2025]. Deterministic network configuration verifiers (Batfish-style analyzers and distributed verifiers) provide feasible oracles for syntactic and workflow correctness properties but prior empirical studies rarely combine preregistration, paired designs, and full archival artifacts at the scale used here [Wang et al., 2025]. Our experiment situates at the intersection: a controlled paired trial using a deterministic verifier as adjudicator and an explicitly bounded repair policy, with full artifact archival for independent verification. This positions our work relative to prior proposals for verifier‑augmented agents and to proposals advocating standardized RAG evaluation in NetOps.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan: The study was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and the analysis executor were frozen before execution (preregistration SHA‑256: aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; a preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was specified as descriptive.
Generation and orchestration: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in execution/model_configuration.json; hash: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with the deterministic verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5. If verification failed, the controller invoked at most one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The baseline condition accepts the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. Provider‑call accounting recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4), consistent with preregistered call budgets and documented in the execution manifest.
Deterministic verifier semantics and codebook: The primary verifier implements a fixed validation pipeline on normalized CLI sequences: (i) syntactic parsing and canonical normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields; all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active/minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison against the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome; the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and boolean valid. The human‑readable verifier codebook (violation‑code → short description) is enumerated in the archived execution manifest; consult the full execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) in the evidence bundle to retrieve the codebook artifact listing and its manifest entry. Representative validator_trace JSON objects are archived under execution/scoring/ and include the verifier fields above. Note: the codebook entry is archived in the execution manifest rather than printed inline here to avoid duplicating provenance metadata; the execution manifest lists the exact verifier codebook artifact path and its SHA‑256 for retrieval.
Repair policy and prompt semantics: If the verifier fails a shared_initial candidate the GVR controller issues at most one repair prompt to the same generation model using a constrained repair template that includes: (a) the original intent abstraction; (b) the verifier violation codes and short descriptions; and (c) a request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. The repair template was intentionally minimal to bound model‑call overhead. A repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid=true for the subsequent candidate. Repair invocations and their acceptance are logged per episode in execution/scoring/ and in the provider traces.
Statistical procedures: Primary confirmatory inference used the conditional exact McNemar, implemented as the two‑sided exact binomial test on discordant pairs. Let n10 = count(success_guarded=1, success_baseline=0) and n01 = count(success_guarded=0, success_baseline=1). The discordant total n = n10 + n01 and the observed favoring‑GVR count k = n10. The two‑sided p‑value is computed as p = 2 * sum_{x=k}^{n} Binom(n, x) * 0.5^{n} (conditional on margins). The preregistered contingency inputs are reported directly from archived artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The paired bootstrap (exploratory) resampled paired outcomes with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) to compute a percentile 95% CI for the paired difference; the bootstrap was declared exploratory because the exact conditional test was the preregistered decision rule. Missingness handling: primary analysis used complete pairs (complete_pair_count = 500); the run recorded zero failed episodes so no imputation was required.
sections.results:
Execution and primary counts: The run completed completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504. analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates; all four repair attempts resulted in subsequent verifier passes and correspond to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008; provider audit fields (deterministic_reconciliation.json) show hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 504, and stage_counts mapping shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4.
Confirmatory exact McNemar calculation: Observed discordants n = n10 + n01 = 4 with k = n10 = 4. The preregistered conditional McNemar two‑sided p‑value is computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). For n = 4, PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 1/16, so p = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because this exact conditional test was the preregistered decision rule, the primary confirmatory claim does not reach preregistered significance.
Exploratory paired bootstrap interval and reconciliation: The exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016]. This bootstrap was pre‑specified as exploratory; the bootstrap can yield a CI excluding zero while the exact conditional McNemar is non‑significant because the conditional McNemar conditions on observed margins and evaluates the binomial tail of discordant outcomes (fixed margins), whereas the bootstrap resamples pairs without fixing margins. With near‑ceiling margins and only four discordants, the bootstrap percentile interval has degraded frequentist coverage and should be interpreted cautiously. We therefore report both outcomes and follow the preregistered decision rule for confirmatory inference.
Representative artifact diagnostics and worked example: Representative scoring JSON objects (execution/scoring/task-00000*-*.json) include validator_trace entries with validation_before, validation_after, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and validator_version = 5.0. A concrete archived example is pair-000001 (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json): the shared_initial candidate, baseline candidate, and guarded candidate are identical and valid; the verifier fields show normalized_configuration = "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 admin up", parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, violation_count = 0, and validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The four repaired episodes (n10) have archived verifier_trace objects showing specific required‑sequence or availability violations that the constrained single repair prompt corrected; these per‑episode traces are archived and indexed in the execution manifest.
Cost accounting and provider audit: Deterministic_reconciliation.json records provider_call_audit: hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 504, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 504, and stage_counts mapping shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4. These counts quantify the incremental generation cost of the bounded repair policy and demonstrate that the experimentally observed repair rate was low relative to the task set size.
Missingness and protocol adherence: The run produced zero failed episodes (failed_episode_count = 0) and complete_pair_count = 500; all preregistered analysis parameters (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729) were used and logged in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and inferential reconciliation: The GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted. Under the preregistered conditional exact McNemar (p = 0.125) this difference is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but is labeled exploratory and interpreted with caution due to small discordant counts. This dual reporting follows the preregistered analytic plan and clarifies how fixed‑margin conditional tests and resampling intervals can diverge in near‑ceiling cases. Practical operational implications: A compact deterministic verifier plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable hazards with low LLM overhead for this synthetic workload. Key operational tradeoffs not covered by the synthetic verifier include verifier runtime and scalability in larger networks, vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing/convergence effects, and hardware resource constraints. Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 is necessary for the experiment’s safety claim but is not sufficient to guarantee production‑level safety across all vendor and timing effects.
Verifier coverage and blind spots: The verifier enforces canonical normalization, workflow sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and exact final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. It does not model vendor idiosyncrasies, protocol timing, control‑plane convergence, or out‑of‑band side effects (e.g., queued control‑plane operations). These limitations are enumerated in the verifier codebook and the execution manifest; expanding verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing models) is required before operational automation. The human‑readable verifier codebook is archived via the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and the manifest lists the codebook artifact entry for retrieval.
Threats to validity: Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, frozen seeds, and complete pairs. Construct validity is limited by the verifier abstraction and synthetic device templates (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1). External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication and real vendor CLI tests are necessary for broader claims. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power calculation assumed a larger baseline discordance (target ≈ 0.08), but the observed near‑ceiling baseline (0.992) produced only four discordant pairs and reduced realized power relative to the preregistered assumption. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; that missing arm prevents completion of the preregistered familywise multiple‑comparison plan.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (which was not executed in this run). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification (representative artifact hashes included below).

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
